title: Kaddish, lived
hookLine: saying Kaddish, or answering amen for others
tomorrow: a candle, a story, or a raised glass: how do you remember someone?

lines: A PRAYER THAT NEVER SAYS DEATH.
SO WHAT IS IT DOING THERE?
cards: At some funerals, someone reads a poem about loss. The prayer Jewish mourners stand and say in synagogue, day after day, has a strange feature: it never mentions death. Not the person who died.
Not grief. Not loss. It's the mourner's prayer, and it's about something else entirely.
So what is it doing there?

teach.b: It opens in Aramaic: yitgadal v'yitkadash sh'mei rabba. Magnified and made holy be His great name. The whole Kaddish praises God's name and asks for peace, and that's the first half of the answer.
At the moment the world feels smallest, the mourner stands up in front of other people and says God's name is great. The second half is the room.
The Kaddish stops in the middle, and everyone answers: amen, y'hei sh'mei rabba m'varach. May His great name be blessed, forever.
Tradition says Kaddish is said with a minyan, a gathering of ten, because it needs people to answer it. The Talmud prizes that answer.
In one story, Elijah tells Rabbi Yose that when people gather in their synagogues and answer "may His great name be blessed," God nods. Another passage praises answering it with all your strength.
So the mourner isn't the only one with a part.
Whoever stands in that room carries half the prayer.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the mourner's prayer never mentions death, and its center is the crowd's reply.

how: Mourners say the Mourner's Kaddish at synagogue services with a minyan, and everyone present answers 'amen, y'hei sh'mei rabba'; some people come to services in part to help make the minyan so others can say it.

o: a prayer praising God's name, said with others
a prayer asking God to rest the dead's soul
a private poem a mourner reads at a grave

p: the ten who make Kaddish possible

s: the mourner's Kaddish is mostly about death and loss
it never mentions death; it praises God's name and asks for peace.
the congregation's answer is at the center of Kaddish
'amen, may His great name be blessed' is the room's part, and the Talmud prizes it.
only mourners have a part when Kaddish is said
everyone in the room answers amen; the answer is half the prayer.

games.q: a shiva house in the evening. nine are gathered, the mourner is waiting to say Kaddish, and you count toward the minyan, but you don't know the prayers well. what fits today's idea?
o: stay and be the tenth; answer amen when the room does.
slip out; the prayers are for the family and people who know them.
wait in the kitchen until someone who knows the words arrives.
games.why: the mourner's Kaddish needs a room that answers. being the tenth, and saying amen, is the whole job; nobody needs to know every word.

practice: Stand up if you can, feet together, the way some people stand for Kaddish. Say only the room's part, slowly: amen, y'hei sh'mei rabba m'varach. If the words are new, the first one is enough.
Then stay standing, quiet, for the rest of the time, as if someone nearby had just finished saying it.

wordCard.voice: Kaddish: the Aramaic prayer that praises God's great name, said by mourners and answered by the room with amen.

orig.note: Aramaic: holy; the prayer that sanctifies God's name.

carryVoice: Keep this: answer amen, because a mourner's words need somewhere to land. Talk to you soon.

sources.ref: The Mourner's Kaddish (traditional Aramaic liturgy; opening and congregational response paraphrased and transliterated)
